\[
\boxed{\,x_n=\frac{2^{a}-1}{2^{a}-2}\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{\varepsilon_k(n)}{2^{ak}},\qquad 
n=\sum_{k\ge 0}\varepsilon_k(n)2^{k},\ \varepsilon_k(n)\in\{0,1\}\,}
\]

**Derivation.**  Since \(a>1\), the series \(\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-ak}\) converges, so each \(x_n\) is well defined (only finitely many \(\varepsilon_k(n)\) are non-zero) and
\[
|x_n|\le \frac{2^{a}-1}{2^{a}-2}\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-ak}
=\frac{2^{a}}{2^{a}-2},
\]
hence \((x_n)\) is bounded.

For distinct \(i,j\), let \(k\) be the smallest index with \(\varepsilon_k(i)\neq\varepsilon_k(j)\); then \(\varepsilon_l(i)=\varepsilon_l(j)\) for all \(l<k\).  Consequently
\[
|x_i-x_j|
\ge \frac{2^{a}-1}{2^{a}-2}\Bigl(2^{-ak}-\sum_{l>k}2^{-al}\Bigr)
= \frac{2^{a}-1}{2^{a}-2}\cdot\frac{1-2^{1-a}}{1-2^{-a}}\,2^{-ak}
=2^{-ak}.
\]
Because \(k=v_2(i-j)\), we have \(|i-j|\ge 2^{k}\), so \(|i-j|^{-a}\le 2^{-ak}\).  Thus
\[
|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^{a}\ge 2^{-ak}\cdot 2^{ak}=1
\]
for every pair \(i\neq j\), as required.

\[
\boxed{x_n=\frac{2^{a}(2^{a}-1)}{2^{a}-2}\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{b_k(n)}{2^{ak}}\qquad(n=0,1,2,\dots),}
\]
where $b_k(n)\in\{0,1\}$ is the $k$-th binary digit of $n$ (so $n=\sum_{k\ge1}b_k(n)2^{k-1}$).

**Derivation.** Set $\lambda=2^{-a}$; since $a>1$ we have $0<\lambda<\tfrac12$. Let $M=\frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda(1-2\lambda)}=\frac{2^{a}(2^{a}-1)}{2^{a}-2}$ and define $x_n=M\sum_{k\ge1}b_k(n)\lambda^k$. Because $\sum_{k\ge1}b_k(n)\lambda^k\le\sum_{k\ge1}\lambda^k=\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}$, we get $|x_n|\le M\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}=\frac{2^{a}}{2^{a}-2}$, so the sequence is bounded.

For distinct $i<j$, let $k$ be the smallest index with $b_k(i)\ne b_k(j)$. Then $b_1,\dots,b_{k-1}$ agree, so $2^{k-1}\mid(j-i)$; hence $j-i\ge2^{k-1}$ and $|j-i|^{-a}\le(2^{k-1})^{-a}=\lambda^{k-1}$. Moreover,
\[
|x_j-x_i|\ge M\Bigl(\lambda^k-\sum_{m>k}\lambda^m\Bigr)
=M\lambda^k\frac{1-2\lambda}{1-\lambda}=\lambda^{k-1},
\]
where the last equality uses the choice of $M$. Thus $|x_j-x_i|\ge\lambda^{k-1}\ge|j-i|^{-a}$, i.e. $|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^{a}\ge1$.

\boxed{x_n=\frac{2^a-1}{1-2^{1-a}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_k(n)}{2^{a(k+1)}}\ \text{where}\ n=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\epsilon_k(n)2^k,\ \epsilon_k(n)\in\{0,1\}}

Write each $n\ge0$ in binary $n=\sum_{k\ge0}\epsilon_k(n)2^k$ ($\epsilon_k\in\{0,1\}$) and set $c_a=\frac{2^a-1}{1-2^{1-a}}$, $x_n=c_a\sum_{k\ge0}\epsilon_k(n)2^{-a(k+1)}$.

**Boundedness.** Since $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-a(k+1)}=\frac{1}{2^a-1}$, we have $0\le x_n\le\frac{c_a}{2^a-1}=\frac{1}{1-2^{1-a}}=\frac{2^{a-1}}{2^{a-1}-1}<\infty$.

**Separation.** For $i\ne j$, let $t=\min\{k:\epsilon_k(i)\ne\epsilon_k(j)\}$. Then $i-j=(\pm1+2m)2^t$ for some integer $m$, so $|i-j|\ge2^t$ and $|i-j|^a\ge2^{at}$. Also
$$|x_i-x_j|\ge c_a\biggl(2^{-a(t+1)}-\sum_{k>t}2^{-a(k+1)}\biggr)
=c_a\cdot2^{-a(t+1)}\frac{1-2^{1-a}}{1-2^{-a}}
=c_a\cdot2^{-at}\frac{1-2^{1-a}}{2^a-1}=2^{-at}.$$
Hence $|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^a\ge2^{-at}\cdot2^{at}=1$ for all distinct $i,j$.

\boxed{\text{Yes. Take }C>\zeta(a)\text{ and define }x_0=0;\text{ inductively choose }x_n\in[-C,C]\setminus\bigcup_{j<n}\bigl(x_j-(n-j)^{-a},\,x_j+(n-j)^{-a}\bigr).}

Since \(a>1\), \(\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-a}=\zeta(a)<\infty\).  
Assume \(x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}\in[-C,C]\) have been chosen so that \(|x_i-x_j|\ge|i-j|^{-a}\) for all \(i<j<n\).  
For \(x_n\), each earlier term \(x_j\) forbids an interval of length \(2(n-j)^{-a}\); the union of these forbidden intervals has total length at most  
\[
2\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{-a}<2\zeta(a)<2C.
\]
Hence the complement in \([-C,C]\) is non-empty, and any choice of \(x_n\) there satisfies \(|x_n-x_j|\ge(n-j)^{-a}\) for all \(j<n\).  
Prior pairs are unaffected, so the condition holds for all distinct indices by induction.  
All terms satisfy \(|x_n|\le C\), so the sequence is bounded and infinite. \(\blacksquare\)
